title: Leaving everything
hook: an estate sale, strangers holding someone's favorite mug; Shantideva on what we leave behind
tomorrow: why confess to someone who already knows?

segments.voice: Last week ended on death may come first: a wrong might outlast the chance to mend it, so mend it now. The verse right after asks a harder question, and it starts with a sale.
screen: `MEND IT NOW.` → `THE NEXT VERSE ASKS MORE.`

segments.voice: The estate sale opens at eight on a Saturday. Strangers drift through a house where someone lived a long life. Green stickers on the dining table. A man turns a coffee mug over to check the price; it's chipped at the handle, the one somebody reached for every morning. In the garage, a box of tools sorted with real care, three dollars for the lot. Two neighbors hold up the same lamp and argue, politely, over who saw it first. And upstairs, in a drawer, a stack of letters about an old family feud that nobody here has heard of. Everything someone guarded, loved, or fought over, sold by the afternoon. So yesterday's question: if you leave it all behind, why fight over any of it?
screen: `GREEN STICKERS, EIGHT A.M.` → `A CHIPPED MUG, THREE DOLLARS.` → `LETTERS ABOUT A FORGOTTEN FEUD.` → `WHY FIGHT OVER ANY OF IT?`

segments.voice: That's Shantideva's question, almost word for word. In the confession chapter he says: I will have to leave everything and go. But not understanding this, I did harm for the sake of friends and for the sake of enemies. Then he looks down the road. Enemies will be gone. Friends will be gone. I'll be gone. Everything will be gone. Whatever I enjoy, he says, turns into a memory, like something seen in a dream. Notice what he does not say. He doesn't say love doesn't matter, or that friends are worthless. He says harm done for their sake, or against an enemy, is the strange part: a lot of damage over things that won't come with anyone. The grudge is the clearest case. It feels like protecting something. Look closely and it's guarding a lamp at an estate sale. That's the freedom inside the verse. Not giving up the people you love, but setting down the fights that won't come with you. I leave it all.
screen: `I WILL HAVE TO LEAVE EVERYTHING.` · `HARM FOR FRIENDS, HARM FOR FOES.` · `LIKE SOMETHING SEEN IN A DREAM.` · `SET DOWN THE FIGHTS, KEEP THE LOVE.` · then, large: `I LEAVE IT ALL.`

segments.voice: Listen for one sound around you: a fridge, traffic, a bird, your own breath. Follow it until it changes or fades. Now bring to mind one small grievance, and let it go the same way, without arguing with it, just letting it pass out of hearing.
Leaving everything: Shantideva's reminder that he'll go without any of it, so harm done for its sake makes no sense.
Your line: I leave it all. Keep the people, set down the fight. Nine days in.

howItsDone: Reflection on impermanence is practiced across Buddhist schools; in the Mahayana, verses like these are often read slowly and turned over in meditation as a way to loosen grudges and grasping.

match.prompt: the verse, piece by piece — tap the pairs.
pairs: and go without any of it
becomes a memory, like a dream
guarding a lamp at an estate sale

myth: the verse teaches that friends and family don't matter
it targets harm done for their sake, not love. keep the people, set down the fight.
Shantideva says whatever he enjoys turns into a memory, like a dream
that's the image he uses for how everything we hold slips into the past.
letting go of a grudge means pretending nothing happened
the verse doesn't erase what happened; it asks why harm someone over what won't last.

fork.setup: your brother borrowed your jacket and returned it with a stain. you've been cold to him for two days. what would Shantideva ask?
options: make him pay for cleaning, so it's fair and you can drop it.
keep the cold shoulder until he apologizes properly.
ask whether a jacket you'll leave behind is worth harm between you, and let it go.
fork.reveal: Shantideva confesses harm done for things he'll leave anyway. the jacket won't come with either of you; the brother is the one who stays.

original.note: Sanskrit: letting go, giving up. A common word for renunciation; the verse itself speaks of leaving everything behind.

trapdoor: what you thought: leaving everything sounds like becoming a monk on a mountain.
what it means: Shantideva says he'll leave it all anyway, so doing harm for its sake, for friends or against foes, makes no sense.
what a scholar hears: the verse links impermanence to confession: harm was done through not understanding this, and seeing it plainly is part of mending.
guess: seeing you'll go without it all, so harm for it is pointless
giving away every possession to live in a monastery
running away from home to find yourself somewhere else

chat.says: ava forgave me for the art show. but she told jess i'm "flaky." still mad. bring it up?
options: Let it go. She forgave the bigger thing, and a grudge won't come with you.
Bring it up so you're even. Then you can both actually move on from it.
Act fine but pull back a little, so she feels what that was like.
chat.meaning: Shantideva says we leave everything behind, so harm over it makes no sense. Keep the friend; set down the fight.

Shantideva.meaning: the Buddhist monk and poet who wrote the Bodhicaryavatara

confession.meaning: chapter two of the poem: owning wrongs openly

estate sale.meaning: a sale of a household's belongings, often after a death
